# Comparison verdict

**The run log does not support "impact-finder improves impact analysis."** On this case the baseline already passes, so the case cannot show improvement; the skill arm is the only arm with a recall miss and it costs more time and tokens.

- **Correctness.** Notes-only: 5/5 runs at recall 1.000 / precision 1.000 against the dependency-cruiser key (229 files). Skill: 4/5 runs at 1.000 / 1.000; run 3 had recall 0.996 (228 of 229 found, no false positives). A baseline that already passes every run leaves no headroom for improvement on this task; the only observed difference in correctness is in the skill's disfavor.
- **Cost of the skill arm (means over 5 runs, same model and tools).**
  - Wall time: 42.0 s vs 32.5 s (about +29%; every skill run slower than every notes-only run).
  - Input tokens: 126,476 vs 55,505 (about 2.3×; range 79k–187k vs 49k–65k).
  - Output tokens: 6,674 vs 5,949 (+12%).
  - Recorded cost: $0.1601 vs $0.1382 per run (+16%; skill run 4 at $0.1297 is the one skill run cheaper than the baseline mean).
- **Variability.** The skill arm is noticeably more variable in input volume (79k–187k) than notes-only (49k–65k); the single recall miss coincided with the highest-token, slowest run. Five runs are not enough to say whether that is a tendency, so treat it as an observation, not a finding.
- **What this does and doesn't show.** A single task is one case. It shows the skill does not beat the pasted notes on this import-graph task; it does not show the skill is worse in general, and it says nothing about cases where the notes are not available to paste. It also says nothing about authoring quality (A), which was not part of this run.

**Release-note recommendation.** Replace "impact-finder improves impact analysis" with a claim the evidence supports, e.g.: *"impact-finder packages the senior engineer's impact-analysis notes as a reusable skill. In a five-run comparison on one task (transitive importers of `src/utils/time.ts`, 229-file dependency-cruiser key), it matched the pasted-notes baseline on 4 of 5 runs (one run missed 1 file) at roughly 2.3× the input tokens, +29% wall time, and +16% cost. # Comparison verdict: impact-finder vs. notes-only baseline

**Verdict: no improvement demonstrated. The release-note claim "impact-finder improves impact analysis" is not supported by this run log and should be withdrawn or reworded.**

Reasoning, per the validation guidance's rule that improvement may be claimed only against a baseline given the same source knowledge without the skill, and that a case the baseline already passes cannot show improvement:

1. **The baseline already passes the case perfectly.** Notes-only scored recall 1.000 / precision 1.000 on all five runs against the 229-file dependency-cruiser key. There is no headroom on this case for the skill to improve correctness; at best it could tie.
2. **The skill did not tie — it was marginally worse on correctness.** Skill run 3 scored recall 0.996 (≈228/229, one dependent file missed) with precision 1.000. Four of five skill runs matched the baseline. On the only measured task-correctness criterion, the skill arm therefore has one failing run where the baseline has none.
3. **The skill arm is consistently slower and more expensive.** Per-run means from the table:

| metric | notes-only (mean of 5) | skill (mean of 5) | difference |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| recall | 1.000 | 0.999 (min 0.996) | −0.001 |
| precision | 1.000 | 1.000 | 0 |
| wall s | 32.5 | 42.0 | +9.5 s (+29%) |
| input tokens | 55,505 | 126,476 | +70,971 (+128%) |
| output tokens | 5,949 | 6,674 | +725 (+12%) |
| cost USD | 0.1382 | 0.1601 | +0.0219 (+16%) |

   Every skill run was slower than every notes-only run (skill min 38.4 s vs. baseline max 34.3 s). Input tokens in the skill arm were higher in all five runs and also far more variable (79k–187k vs. 49k–65k). The one skill run cheaper than the baseline (run 4, $0.1297) still took longer and consumed more input tokens; the cost figures are reported as logged and were not independently reconciled against token counts.
4. **This is one case, repeated — not a set of held-out cases.** All ten runs used the same target module (`src/utils/time.ts`). Five repetitions establish run-to-run variability on this input; they do not establish generalization to other modules, larger transitive closures, re-exports/barrel files, type-only imports, or dynamic imports — the situations where a senior engineer's judgment would plausibly matter. The log does not record whether this case was used while authoring or tuning the skill; if it was, it is development evidence, not independent evidence.

What the data *does* support: both arms, given the same expert notes, can reproduce a dependency-cruiser transitive-importer list for this module with near-perfect accuracy; the skill packaging added cost and latency without adding correctness on this case.

# impact-finder — comparison verdict and B result record

## Verdict

The supplied run log does not support the release-note sentence "impact-finder improves impact analysis." Change it.

Reason, per the validation guidance: an improvement can only be claimed against a baseline given the same source knowledge without the skill, and a case that such a baseline already passes cannot show improvement. The notes-only baseline passed this case on all five runs (recall 1.000, precision 1.000 against the 229-file dependency-cruiser key). The skill arm matched it on four runs and fell short on one (run 3, recall 0.996 — one of 229 files omitted; no false positives). On the secondary measures the skill arm was uniformly worse: mean wall time 42.0 s vs 32.5 s, mean input tokens about 126,500 vs about 55,500 (peak 187,263 vs 65,176), mean output tokens about 6,670 vs about 5,950, mean cost $0.160 vs $0.138 (the skill was cheaper on only one of five runs).

On this evidence the skill shows no correctness gain over the notes alone, one unexplained recall miss, and a consistent cost of roughly 2.3x input tokens and about 10 s per run. The cause of the run-3 omission is not established by the log and should not be stated as known.

Suggested replacement wording for the release note:

> impact-finder packages the impact-analysis notes as a reusable skill. On the one evaluated task (direct and transitive importers of `src/utils/time.ts`, 229-file dependency-cruiser key) it matched the full answer in 4 of 5 runs and missed one file in the fifth; the same notes pasted directly matched in 5 of 5 runs at lower latency and token cost. No improvement over the notes is demonstrated. Behavior on other modules and repositories is untested.

# B evaluation plan: `impact-finder`

Scope of this document: a plan only. Nothing below has been run; no fixtures exist yet; no results are claimed. The generated skill is evaluated as supplied (the four-step SKILL.md above, no `references/` or `scripts/`), so it must stand on its own text plus the executor's ordinary file and shell tools.

## 1. What B is testing

B asks whether a fresh executor, given only a realistic request, a TypeScript repository, and this SKILL.md, produces a correct impact list. It does not test whether the host picks `impact-finder` out of the ~40 installed skills — that is a discovery check (A-side), covered separately in §7. It also does not test the author's faithfulness to the source material; the skill's own text is the only authority here.

## 2. Setup

**Executor context.** A fresh session per case. Supply only:
- the task request (natural phrasing, see cases),
- the fixture repository on disk,
- `impact-finder/SKILL.md` as the installed skill (either loaded by the host or passed explicitly — record which; explicit loading proves nothing about automatic selection),
- ordinary read/search tools (file read, grep/rg, directory listing). Optionally `tsc --noEmit` or `node` if the host normally provides them; record the allowed tool set.

Exclude: this plan, `work-to-skill`, the authoring guide, expected answers, any prior run's output, and any reviewer commentary.

**Fixtures.** Small synthetic TypeScript repositories, built for this evaluation in an isolated directory (new, empty, not the shared skills folder), with no real project code. Because they are synthetic and small, the expected importer graph can be derived by construction and double-checked by one independent mechanical method (e.g., a `madge`/`dependency-cruiser` run, or a one-off script using the TypeScript compiler API that resolves imports with the fixture's `tsconfig.json`). The script lives outside the fixture directory and is pointed at the fixture by path argument. Expected graphs are evaluator-only material.

**Fresh-case rule.** None of these fixtures may have been used while writing or revising the skill. If the skill is revised after a run, the cases used to diagnose the failure become development evidence; a held-out claim requires a new fixture.

**Repeats.** One run per case by default. Repeat only where output varies materially between runs (e.g., hop assignment of re-exported symbols) and the variance would change a pass/fail judgment.

## 4. Cases

Each case is a separate fixture + request. Expected results are kept in the evaluator record only.

**B1 — Supported success.** `src/lib/money.ts` exports `formatCents`. Imported directly by `src/components/Price.tsx` and `src/lib/money.test.ts`; `Price.tsx` imported by `src/pages/checkout.tsx`; `checkout.tsx` imported by `src/App.tsx`. Request: *"What is affected if I change the signature of formatCents in src/lib/money.ts?"* Checks C1, C2, C4, C6, C8, C10, C12. Expected: 3 hops, 5 files, one marked test.

**B2 — Aliases and barrel re-export.** `tsconfig.json` with `"@/*": ["src/*"]`. `src/utils/index.ts` re-exports from `./slug`. Importers use `@/utils`, `@/utils/slug`, and a relative `../utils`. Request: *"Which files import src/utils/slug.ts?"* Checks C1–C4. Expected: all three import styles present; barrel hop convention recorded, not judged.

**B3 — Unresolvable imports.** Fixture includes: `const m = await import(\`./plugins/${name}\`)`; a `.js` file with `require('../src/core')`; an import of a module that does not exist on disk; an `.mdx` page importing a component. Request: *"What breaks if I rename the exports of src/core.ts?"* Checks C5, C2 (nothing fabricated for the plugin glob), C11.

**B4 — Cycle.** `a.ts` ↔ `b.ts` mutual import, both imported by `c.ts`. Request on `a.ts`. Checks C9, C1.

**B5a — Step-4 boundary (should not walk).** Request: *"In src/lib/money.ts I'm renaming the local helper `pad2` to `padTwo` — it isn't exported. What's affected?"* Checks C7, C12. Expected: file read, answer that only that file is touched, no repository walk. Asking a clarifying question about whether `pad2` is really unexported is acceptable.

**B5b — Step-4 boundary (should walk).** Same fixture, request: *"Small change in src/lib/money.ts: formatCents now returns a `Money` object instead of a string."* Checks C8. Expected: full walk despite the word "small".

**B6 — Out of scope.** A Python-only fixture, request phrased identically to B1. Checks C11, C12. Expected: states the skill/approach applies to TypeScript imports and either stops or bounds what it can do; no invented importer list.

**B7 (optional, if time) — Type-only imports and monorepo.** `import type { Money }` importers; a `packages/*` workspace where `@acme/money` resolves via workspace paths. Checks C1, C3. Treat results as advisory information about depth unless the fixture's tsconfig makes resolution unambiguous.

**Baseline (for any improvement claim).** Run B1, B2, B3, B5a in a fresh context *without* the skill, same model, host, and tools. An improvement claim is valid only for cases the baseline fails and the skilled run passes. If the baseline already passes B1, B1 shows correctness but not improvement.

Keep all expected answers and this record outside the fixture directories and outside the installable skill folder.

## 6. What passing means

- **Case pass:** all required criteria applicable to that case are pass. Advisory criteria (C4 convention, C6 heuristic, C10) are reported separately and never flip a case result.
- **Overall B pass:** B1–B6 all pass. B7 is informational.
- **Overall B fail:** any required failure in any case. A missed importer (C1), a fabricated importer (C2), a silently dropped unresolvable import (C5), a repository walk on B5a or a failure to walk on B5b (C7/C8), or any side-effecting action (C12) fails regardless of how good the other output looks; no aggregate score offsets these.
- **Unverified:** any required criterion not run, not observable (e.g., no tool trace available for C7/C12), or whose host/model differs from the one claimed. An unverified required criterion blocks any "verified" claim; report the skill as behavior-unverified for that criterion and name what evidence is missing.
- **Compatibility:** claim only for the host(s), model(s), and tool sets actually used. A run on one host says nothing about another.

On a required failure: repair SKILL.md narrowly for the demonstrated defect (for example, if C7 fails, step 4 may need a definition of "change inside one file"), re-run the failing case and the adjacent boundary case (B5a with B5b, B3 with B1), and build a new fixture for any held-out claim. Do not update the copy in the shared skills folder until the recheck passes; the copy currently under review should not be installed until B is at least run on B1, B3, and B5a/B5b.

# Decision

**We cannot say v2 improves the skill on this evidence.** The honest statement is: on 8 held-out synthetic contracts with 2 runs each, v2 passed more runs than v1 (15/16 vs 13/16), which is directionally favorable but not sufficient for an improvement claim. Reasons, taken from the supplied guidance:

1. **Observed variability is as large as the measured difference.** Both versions pass and fail the *same contract* across runs (v1: C2, C4, C7; v2: C6). That shows run-to-run noise of roughly one run per contract. The entire v1→v2 gap is 2 runs out of 16, within that noise band. The guidance says to repeat when observed variability warrants it; it does here, and 2 runs per cell is not enough to separate the version effect from the noise.

2. **v2 shows a failure v1 did not.** C6 passed both v1 runs and failed one v2 run. Until the C6 output is inspected, this cannot be distinguished from a regression introduced by the rewritten paragraph. An aggregate count cannot offset a lost condition or exception; if the C6 failure is a planted problem v1 caught and v2 now misses, that is material regardless of the 15/16.

3. **No link is recorded between the failures and the changed behavior.** The revision touched one paragraph on indemnity caps. The record does not say which contracts planted an indemnity-cap problem, or whether each failure was a missed flag or a spurious flag. Without that, the 2-run gain cannot be attributed to the change rather than to noise, and the C6 loss cannot be ruled in or out as a regression.

4. **Comparable conditions are not recorded.** Host, model, allowed tools, fresh executor context, and whether pass/fail was judged mechanically or by a model are not stated. An improvement claim requires comparable conditions; these are unverified.

5. **Neither version meets the B criterion overall.** The criterion is required per contract (flag every planted problem and nothing else). v2 has a required failure (C6 run 2), so v2's B result is **fail**, not a near-pass. v1 fails on C2, C4, C7.

6. **I did not inspect anything.** I have only the summary table. The record below documents supplied results; it does not confirm that runs occurred as described or that pass/fail judgments were correct.

What would support a claim: inspect the four failed run outputs (v1 C2r2, C4r1, C7r1; v2 C6r2) and record what was missed or over-flagged and whether it touched indemnity caps; add repetitions on the contracts that showed variance and on any contract with a planted indemnity-cap problem; record host/model/tools and confirm they were identical across versions; keep these 8 contracts as held-out only if no further revision is made from these results — if v3 is tuned on them, they become development evidence and a fresh set is needed for the next claim.

**No — the supplied results do not support claiming that v2 improves the skill.** They support a weaker statement: on these 8 contracts, v2 performed at least as well as v1 in aggregate, and the difference (2 runs out of 16) is within the run-to-run variation both versions show.

1. **Improvement must be shown against the previous version under comparable conditions, and a case the baseline already passes cannot show improvement.** v1 passes every one of the 8 contracts in at least one run. Every differing contract differs by exactly one run, and the same version flips its own outcome on repeated runs of the same contract. That is the signature of executor nondeterminism, not of a version difference.

2. **Repeat only where variability warrants — and here it does.** Two runs per contract were enough to reveal variability but not enough to separate the versions from it. A 13/16 vs 15/16 split is roughly what chance alone produces when both versions have the same underlying pass rate (by hand, with 4 total failures across 32 runs distributed at random, v2 ending up with ≤1 of them happens about 30% of the time; this is my own arithmetic, not a computed check).

3. **The change was a rewrite of one paragraph about indemnity caps, but the table does not say which contracts plant indemnity-cap problems or why any run failed.** Without that, the three v1 failures cannot be attributed to the paragraph that changed, and the v2 failure on C6 cannot be classified as either noise or a regression introduced by the rewrite (e.g., a new false flag — "nothing else" is part of the pass condition). A single unexplained v2 failure on a contract v1 passed twice is exactly the kind of item that should block an improvement claim until inspected.

4. **Held-out status is stated but not evidenced.** The contracts are described as "new," which I take as held-out. If the C2/C4/C7 failures (or anything about these contracts) motivated the indemnity-cap rewrite, they are development evidence and cannot carry an independent improvement claim.

It does not cover A (authoring fidelity, which here is also uncertain: the skill carries no provenance for its rules, so treat them as the author's procedure) or automatic discovery among the ~40 installed skills. Both are noted at the end as separate checks to run before the copy. Nothing below has been run; everything is a plan to execute.

## 1. Setup

**Executor context.** A fresh agent session per case. Supply only: the task request, the synthetic repository in an isolated directory, the `impact-finder` SKILL.md, and whatever read/search tools the shared agent normally has (file read, glob, grep, shell read-only). Withhold the authoring conversation, `work-to-skill`, this plan, the ground truth, and any hints. Record the exact tool set granted; if it differs from the production agent's tools, the result is for the tested condition only.

**Ground truth built before any run.** The evaluator constructs each synthetic repo by hand so the import graph is known by design, not inferred afterward. Write down for each case: the target module, the complete set of direct importers, each transitive layer, which files are tests, which are pages/routes, and which imports are deliberately unresolvable. Optionally cross-check the designed graph with a dependency tool (`madge`, `tsc --listFiles`, or a script) on the evaluator side only; if no such tool is available, say so and treat the hand-built graph as the sole reference. Repos are synthetic; no real project code, paths, or names.

**Cases must be new.** None of the repos below may have been used to write or tune the skill. If the skill is revised after seeing results, these cases become development evidence and a further held-out case is needed before claiming the revision works.

# Decision

**We cannot say v2 improves the skill on this evidence.** We can say v2 was observed to pass 15/16 runs versus v1's 13/16 on the same 8 held-out contracts, and that this difference has not been shown to exceed run-to-run variability or to come from the rewritten indemnity-cap paragraph.

Reasons, from the supplied guidance:

1. **The difference is inside the observed variability.** No contract fails consistently under either version. Every v1 failure (C2, C4, C7) is on a contract v1 also passed once; v2's only failure (C6) is on a contract v2 also passed once. Both versions show single-run flips; v1 flipped on 3 contracts, v2 on 1. With two runs per contract, a difference of two runs out of sixteen does not separate the change from noise. The guidance says to repeat when observed variability warrants it, and it does here.
2. **Attribution to the change is unrecorded.** The revision is one paragraph about indemnity caps. The record does not say which contracts have planted indemnity-cap problems, or what each failed run did wrong (missed a planted clause vs. flagged something extra). Without that, the C2/C4/C7 gains cannot be tied to the change, and the C6 failure cannot be classified as a regression caused by the change or an unrelated flip.
3. **A required failure is present.** The pass criterion ("every planted problem and nothing else") is a required mechanical criterion. v2 run 2 on C6 fails it. v2's overall B result is therefore **fail on C6** and **pass** on the other seven, not an unqualified pass; and C6 was a contract v1 passed twice, so it must be inspected before v2 is treated as at least as good as v1.
4. **Cases that both versions always pass carry no improvement evidence.** C1, C3, C5, C8 (8 of 16 runs each) are ties and only show no regression was observed there.
5. **Comparability is asserted, not recorded.** Host, model, tool access, fresh executor context, and exclusion of authoring material are not stated for either version. The improvement claim requires comparable conditions; these are unverified from the supplied text.
